work_order.root_cause: PR #50 added a blanket vi.restoreAllMocks() to index.test.ts's afterEach and, separately, wrote a comment that claims more than the code does. The blanket restore reaches beyond the console spy it targeted because vi.restoreAllMocks() is file-scoped rather than spy-scoped, so it silently takes the file's global.fetch spy down after the first test. The comment was written from the shape of the teardown rather than from what each test actually registers: it speaks of 'a mocked console.log' as though all tests mocked one (five of ten do) and of 'an open handle' as though every openDatabase() handle were closed (one test pushes any). Both halves of one sentence over-generalised the same way, so both are narrowed — and both are counted against the describe as it will exist AFTER this change appends a tenth test to it, which is what the second rejection caught in v3.
work_order.approach:
Three small edits across the two files PR #50 touched, plus one regression test that fails without the fix. I applied the whole thing, ran it in both directions, and restored the tree.

The fetch patch moves from once-per-file to once-per-test. Hoist the baseURL template literal (computed inside the beforeAll at index.test.ts:16) to a module-scope const, keep patchFetchForSqlJS(baseURL) in the beforeAll where init({ baseURL }) needs it, and add a top-level beforeEach calling patchFetchForSqlJS(baseURL) again. patchFetchForSqlJS is vi.spyOn(global, 'fetch').mockImplementation(...) with no internal restore, so re-spying a restored global is idempotent and the afterEach's blanket restore can no longer outrun it. This is the smaller of the two fixes the review offered; the other, narrowing the restore to the console spy alone, would mean hand-tracking which spies exist at teardown time and would break the deliberate mirroring of index.electron.test.ts's teardown().

A new test appended at the end of the describe asserts vi.isMockFunction(globalThis.fetch) is true. It must be last, and I measured all three modes: last-position full run fails without the fix, passes with it, and `-t` filtering that selects the test alone PASSES EVEN WITHOUT THE FIX ('1 passed | 15 skipped (16)'), because the beforeAll patch is still standing when nothing else has run. The comment above the test states this, matching the convention argued at index.electron.test.ts:129-137.

The comment at index.test.ts:28-31 is rewritten so each half carries its true scope, every count stated against the post-change describe of ten tests. The exact text is supplied in files[0].change and was applied verbatim: 80 columns maximum, none of the seven phrases the ban list names.

This version exists mainly to mend v4's defect: AC-4 banned the bare word 'nine' while the mandated, and true, sentence 'Eight of the other nine call openDatabase() without registering the handle' contains it. Per the rejection's required fix, AC-4 now bans 'nine tests' instead and states the bare word 'nine' is required; files[0].change (b) and qa_script step 8 are swept to the identical seven phrases. I also renamed the new test from '...for every test, not just the first' to '...for each test, not just the first', because the old title itself contained a banned phrase — the same defect one level down. With both edits the whole file matches none of the seven, so the check holds whether QA greps the comment or the file.

The Mirrors sentence attributes the both-halves claim to 'each of that file's three tests' rather than 'every test'.

In index.electron.test.ts:143 'above' becomes 'below'. One word. That file's own comment at lines 23-26 is deliberately left alone: there both claims are true of all three of its tests.

Implementation note: oxfmt collapses a wrapped arrow-body expression to the single line `it('...', () => expect(...).toBe(true));`. I wrote it on one line; oxfmt reported 'All matched files use the correct format' and `yarn lint` and `yarn typecheck` both pass with the whole change applied.

No production code changes. No new dependency.

work_order.debate_summary:
plan/brief.md records no decisions for this issue — the 'Decided for this issue' section is empty. The only pipeline-authored input is the recorded rejection of v4, which raised one objection; it is answered directly at its source in all three places it named, not worked around.

Objection: AC-4 forbade the literal 'nine' anywhere in the rewritten comment, but the replacement text files[0].change mandates — and which is TRUE of the shipped file — contains 'Eight of the other nine call openDatabase() without registering the handle', so a faithful implementation failed the criterion QA holds it to, on every attempt. The rejection's required repair was explicit: align AC-4's ban with the other two lists by banning 'nine tests' rather than bare 'nine' (keeping 'five of the nine', 'the other four' and 'every test'), state positively that the bare word 'nine' is REQUIRED, and sweep the same clause through files[0].change (b) and qa_script step 8 so all three read identically. I did exactly that. All three now carry the same seven-phrase ban list, and all three state that 'Eight of the other nine call openDatabase() without registering the handle' is required. I verified it mechanically rather than by reading: the shipped comment, extracted with the awk command AC-4 now mandates, returns 0 for each of the seven banned phrases and exactly 1 occurrence of bare 'nine'.

I also did what the rejection asked 'at the source' more broadly, and found one more instance of the same defect that v4 missed: v4's mandated test title, 'keeps the sql.js wasm fetch patched for every test, not just the first', contains the banned phrase 'every test' itself, so a whole-file grep would have failed a correct implementation even after the AC-4 fix. The title is now '...for each test, not just the first', and I confirmed the whole file matches none of the seven phrases at either the comment or whole-file scope — so the check now passes whichever way QA applies it.

Nothing else in v4 was inherited unverified: I applied the whole change to this checkout and re-ran everything. Baseline 15 passed; with the fix 16 passed and the sqlite file reports 10 tests; deleting only the beforeEach gives '× keeps the sql.js wasm fetch patched for each test', 'expected false to be true', '1 failed | 15 passed (16)'; the -t vacuity reproduces at '1 passed | 15 skipped (16)'; the electron file gives '2 passed | 1 expected fail (3)'; yarn lint reports 'All matched files use the correct format' and yarn typecheck 'success: 10, aborted: 0'; the post-change greps return ten it() blocks, five console mocks, two handle pushes and ten openDatabase calls with none in the new test.

Two inherited traps are corrected and warned about in AC-4 and qa_script: the `vi\.spyOn(console` form matches only four of the five console spies because one site is a wrapped call, and the issue review's own 'six sites' figure is really five. One claim I did NOT re-measure this session is the first-position probe; the evidence above rests on the last-position full run, which I measured in both directions. Finding 4 remains deferred: PR #50 is MERGED and .github/** is forbidden, so no ticket can carry it.
residual_risks: The new test asserts a vitest internal (vi.isMockFunction on a global) rather than application behaviour. It is a guard on the teardown contract this file relies on, and the only assertion in the file that would notice the fetch patch lapsing; if a future vitest changes isMockFunction semantics the test would need rewriting.

The new test has no power in an isolated (-t) run, and nothing enforces its position mechanically — a future refactor that moves it earlier, or a CI change that filters tests individually, would neuter it silently. It is caught only by a human reading the comment, by qa_script step 5, or by AC-1's ten-hit `^  it\(` count noticing it is no longer last.

The rewritten comment's factual halves can still drift if someone later adds handles.push to another test, or a console.log spy to a sixth, without updating it. AC-4 pins the current state with greps rather than adding an observer to keep it honest, so drift is caught at QA time, not prevented at write time.

AC-4's ban list is now seven specific phrases rather than a general prohibition on over-claiming. It catches the over-claims this ticket is about, but a re-broadened claim phrased differently ('both halves cover the file', say) would pass it. The greps in the same criterion are what actually pin the counts; the phrase list only guards the specific wordings v1-v4 produced.

AC-1 through AC-6 are all verify:'test'. There is no browser-observable surface to this ticket — it touches only two unit-test files — so no criterion is checkable against a live URL and none is written as if it were.

AC-4 is the only criterion that rests on a human reading a comment against a grep. It is checkable, and its counts are now mechanically pinned at two scopes, but a QA agent that skips the greps and accepts the comment on sight would not catch a re-broadened claim.
